title: Why Does Red Mean Stop? (The First Traffic Light Exploded)
parts: The world's first traffic light exploded less than a month after it was switched on.
The police officer operating it was injured.
Today, we obey its descendants every single day without a second thought.
Red means stop. Green means go. But who decided that?
To find out, we have to go back to London, and to the age of horses.
Picture London in the 1860s. No cars. Just streets packed with horse-drawn carriages, and people on foot.
Outside the Houses of Parliament, crossing the road was a risky business.
A railway man named John Peake Knight had an idea: control the street the way railways control trains.
By day, his signal had two arms, like a railway signal. Arms level meant stop. Arms lowered meant proceed with caution.
At night, it used red and green gas lamps.
A police officer worked it by hand, with a lever.
It went up in December 1868.
Then, in early January 1869, gas leaked, and one of the lamps exploded.
The officer was badly injured, and the signal was taken down.
Not the best product launch.
Traffic lights did not come back to Britain for about sixty years.
So where did those colours come from? From the railways.
In January 1841, Parliament was investigating a string of railway accidents, so the managers met to agree on signals.
At that meeting, the managers agreed to adopt the colours of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway: red for danger, white for safe, and green for caution.
Why red? Nobody knows for sure. Red already felt like danger, so it was a natural choice.
But white turned out to be a bad idea. If a red lens broke, a danger signal would suddenly show white, the colour for safe.
So over time, some railways moved to green for go.
You may have heard another story: that red is used because it cuts through fog.
It sounds clever, but it is a myth.
Fog scatters all colours about equally.
Red seems to have won because of history, not nature.
More than forty years after London's explosion, the idea came back, this time with electricity.
Among the first electric lights was one built by a Salt Lake City police officer named Lester Wire, in 1912.
Then in 1914, Cleveland put one up on a busy corner.
But early signals only had two colours, red and green, with nothing in between.
In 1920, a Detroit police officer named William Potts added a third light: amber, for caution.
Railways already had caution signals, so the idea was easy to borrow.
So that is the whole story. Red came from the railways, and the amber light came from a Detroit police officer.
And the whole idea began with a lamp that blew up outside Parliament.
The most ordinary spot on your commute has a surprisingly wild backstory.
Now picture the light turning green. You hit the gas and say, "OK, let's go."
But what does "OK" actually stand for?
And why does the whole world say it?
